newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia will allow 500,000 T '97 wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia will allow 500,000 T '97 wheat exports.

text.p: Yugoslavia will allow up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat to be exported this year but not before the harvest ends, a senior government official said on Wednesday.
"There are no trade barriers for wheat except for an export quota set at 500,000 tonnes this year," undersecretary in the federal Agriculture Ministry Milan Prostran said.
"But it is only a formal framework figure as export permissions will be issued after the post-harvest wheat balances are established," he told Reuters.
Prostran's opinion was that no exports should be allowed prior to the wheat autumn sowing.
"We cannot afford a repetition of 1996 when we exported and then had to import wheat to feed the people," he said.
Analysts believe that after a 25-year record low 1996 crop of 1.5 million tonnes of wheat, the state's silos are empty despite some 300,000 tonnes of wheat imports.
The government keeps figures on stocks a secret.

Official preliminary 1997 wheat crop forecasts are set at 2.8 million tonnes from an area of some 800,000 hectares, 217,000 ha up on harvested area in 1996. The average expected yield is seen at 3.44 tonnes per ha.
But heavy storms and rainfalls in the past few days have halted harvesting in the country's granary Vojvodina in the north and slowed down harvesters in the central part of the country.
"Wheat is sensitive especially in its final stage of ripening. Rain will reduce yields and effect grain quality," said Miroslav Malesevic of the Novi Sad Institute for Crop Farming.
If the wheat is ripe, 10 litres of rainfall per square metre causes a crop loss of 300-400 kilos per hectare, he said.
"It is very difficult to estimate the damage caused by the bad weather in the past four days, but yields per hectare could be by 200-300 kilos lower (in the area of rainfall)."
Malesevic said the Institute's forecast of more than 3.5 tonnes of wheat per hectare, and from 3.5 to four tonnes per hectare in Vojvodina, was more optimistic than the official statistics.
According to statistics, Vojvodina is expected to produce 1.36 million tonnes of wheat from 356,000 ha under wheat.
Malesevic said wheat yields in Vojvodina could drop to below the official forecast of 3.82 tonnes per hectare.
Another wheat expert, Rozika Vukobratovic of the Novi Sad Institute for Wheat and Flour Technology, warned on secondary problems arising after the rains.
"The harvest slow-down will increase the costs. And rains will speed up growth of weeds," she said and added:
"Another problem is unexpected quantities of smutty grains which appeared on ten various places throughout the country."
Vukobratovic refused to disclose any figures, but said it was much more widespread than the previous years and had to be put under control as smutty grains could not be used for bread.

Analysts disagree on the quantity of wheat needed for domestic use which ranges from two to 2.4 million tonnes, but most believe that some 500,000 tonnes of good quality '97 wheat crop could be available for export regardless of the damages. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
